displayQuote: Writing free verse is like playing tennis with the net down

meta.title: Who really said "Writing free verse is like playing tennis with the net down"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Frost really said it, more than once and in more than one wording. But the 1935 address everyone cites as its source has never been documented.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Writing free verse is like playing tennis with the net down'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuinely Robert Frost. The 1935 Milton Academy citation attached to it has no contemporary record; the earliest is a 1933 lecture report.

answer.label: Spoken by Robert Frost
answer.sourceLine: This one is real. Frost made the comparison for decades and in more than one form: Quote Investigator ↗ traces it from a February 1933 lecture in Scranton, Pennsylvania — where he likened free verse to “playing tennis without a net or handball without a wall” — through a 1934 letter to his daughter Lesley, to this exact wording, printed in Reginald L. Cook’s 1945 article in College English. The source usually bolted onto it, an address at Milton Academy on 17 May 1935, is a different matter: reference works and Wikiquote ↗ repeat it, and Quote Investigator says flatly that it has “not yet acquired contemporary documentation supporting the above citation”. So we credit the line and decline the footnote.

source.excerpt: “Writing free verse is like playing tennis with the net down.”
trail: Quote Investigator’s chronology of the simile ↗ is the anchor for this page. Its earliest match is a report in The Scranton Times of 10 February 1933 (p. 22, col. 6) of a Frost reading at the Century Club, which has him likening free verse, “which he said he never writes, to playing tennis without a net or handball without a wall”. A second Scranton paper covered the same evening. QI concludes that Frost “did use a simile on multiple occasions that equated writing free verse to playing tennis with the net down (or without a net)”.

The exact sentence on this page is documented in a scholarly article published in Frost’s lifetime: QI cites ↗ Reginald L. Cook, “Robert Frost: A Time to Listen”, College English, volume 7, number 2 (November 1945), starting at page 66, with the line at page 69. We could not open the journal itself — it sits behind a paywall our fetcher is blocked from — so this rests on QI’s transcription rather than on our own reading of page 69.

Wikiquote’s sourced section for Frost ↗ carries this wording and sources it to an “Address at Milton Academy, Massachusetts (May 17, 1935)”. That date is also in the Encarta Book of Quotations and The Columbia Dictionary of Quotations. None of them prints a contemporary record of the address, and QI says it has not found one either. We repeat the claim as a claim.

Frost kept returning to the image. QI records it again in The New York Times in January 1939, a Colorado paper in April 1939, The Brattleboro Daily Reformer in August 1941, and the 1966 collection Interviews with Robert Frost ↗ for a 1959 interview — each time slightly re-cut. That is what a favourite line of a working talker looks like in the record.
source.excerptNote: The 1934 letter is the closest thing to a manuscript original, and it is longer and less quotable than the version that survived: as Quote Investigator quotes it from the University of Virginia catalogue ↗, Frost wrote “For my part I should be as satisfied to play tennis with the net down as to write verse with no verse form set to stay me.” The famous sentence is that thought, filed down.

source.rightsNote: In copyright in the United States. Every documented appearance of this remark falls after the 1930 public-domain cutoff: the 1933 newspaper reports, the 1934 letter (recorded in a 1974 University of Virginia catalogue) and the 1945 College English article, itself under copyright to the National Council of Teachers of English. Frost died in 1963 and his literary estate holds his words. His pre-1931 books — A Boy’s Will, North of Boston, Mountain Interval — are a different matter and are freely readable, but this sentence is not in any of them.

author.name: Robert Frost
author.heading: About Robert Frost
author.bio: Robert Frost wrote plain-spoken New England poems inside strict metre and rhyme, and won four Pulitzer Prizes doing it. He spent the decades after returning to America in 1915 writing, teaching and lecturing — which is why so many of his best-known sentences are things he said in a hall rather than things he published. He read at John F. Kennedy’s inauguration in 1961, two years before he died.

misattribution.heading: What people get wrong about it
misattribution.intro: Nobody has stolen this line from Frost — it is his. What travels with it is a source line that has never been checked, and a rival wording that is equally genuine.

items.who: An address at Milton Academy, 17 May 1935
items.why: Printed in the Encarta Book of Quotations, The Columbia Dictionary of Quotations and Wikiquote ↗, and copied outward from there. Quote Investigator ↗ states that it has “not yet acquired contemporary documentation supporting the above citation”. The address may well have happened; the sentence is simply not tied to it by any record anyone has produced.

Two years before the Milton date, QI’s earliest located match ↗ has Frost telling a Scranton audience that free verse is like “playing tennis without a net or handball without a wall”. If you want a first documented outing, this is it — not 1935.
Not a corruption. QI ↗ finds both forms in Frost’s mouth across three decades and concludes he “employed variable phrasing”. Quoting either one is defensible; claiming one is the original is not.

misattribution.truthLine: The safe form of the claim: Robert Frost said this, repeatedly, from at least February 1933 — as Quote Investigator documents ↗. Where and when he first said it in exactly these words is not established, and the 1935 address usually named has no record behind it.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Frost was arguing with the whole direction of modern poetry, and he made the argument in one sentence a sportswriter could use. Free verse had been the advancing position since Whitman and was the settled avant-garde by the 1920s; Frost, working in blank verse and rhyme, needed a way to say that constraint is not an obstacle to the game but the thing that makes it a game at all.

It worked because it concedes nothing and explains everything. The net is not in the tennis player’s way — without it there is no score, no difficulty, no reason to watch. Whether you think that is fair to free verse or a caricature of it, it is the line by which the argument against the form is now remembered, and it was said by a man who was on a lecture circuit and knew exactly how a line travels.
context.pull: The net is not in the player’s way. Without it there is no game.
